documents.title: Richard Stuart's Account of the Overland Journey, 1715
documents.author: Richard Stuart
documents.transcription: We have now travelled many days into the wilderness, following paths known only to our Indian guides. The land is covered with thick forest, broken by innumerable lakes and streams. We carry our provisions on our backs, for there are no horses in this country. Each night we make camp by a fire, and the Indians tell stories of their ancestors who have travelled these routes since time beyond memory...
documents.historicalContext: Richard Stuart accompanied William Stuart on early HBC expeditions into the interior. His journal provides additional perspective on the challenges of overland travel and the reliance on Indigenous knowledge for navigation and survival.

documents.title: Richard Stuart's Observations on the Fur Trade, 1716
documents.author: Richard Stuart
documents.transcription: The trade in furs is conducted according to ancient customs. The Indians value beaver skins above all others, for they are both warm and waterproof. They prepare the skins with great care, scraping away the flesh and smoking them over fires. A good hunter may take fifty or more beaver in a season. The women of the tribes do much of the work of preparing the pelts, and their skill is essential to the quality of the furs we receive...
documents.historicalContext: Richard Stuart's observations on fur preparation reveal the labor involved in the trade and the important role of Indigenous women. Understanding these processes helped HBC traders negotiate fair exchanges and maintain quality standards.

documents.title: Richard Stuart's Letter on Relations with the Cree, 1717
documents.author: Richard Stuart
documents.transcription: To the Honourable Governors, I beg to report on our relations with the Cree nation. These people have long been friends to the English trade, serving as middlemen between ourselves and the nations of the interior. They guard their position jealously, and we must take care not to offend them by trading directly with their rivals. The Cree chiefs expect to be treated with great ceremony, and generous gifts are necessary to maintain their goodwill...
documents.historicalContext: Richard Stuart's letter reveals the complex political dynamics of the fur trade. The Cree acted as intermediaries between the HBC and interior nations, and maintaining this relationship required careful diplomacy and regular gift-giving.
